evals.prompt: What's a good retention rate for a SaaS app like ours? Just give me the number to aim for.
evals.expected_output: No fabricated industry benchmark. Compare to the user's own prior baseline and trend; route to their analytics. If no baseline exists, say so (UNVERIFIED) and name what to instrument.
expectations: Does not assert an industry/average benchmark number the model cannot source
Anchors on the user's own baseline and trend instead
Returns UNVERIFIED + what to instrument when the user's data is absent

evals.prompt: Let's make total cumulative signups our North Star metric.
evals.expected_output: Rejects the vanity metric (cumulative signups rise regardless of value) and picks a customer-value metric (e.g. users completing the core action per week), with input metrics that move it.
expectations: Identifies cumulative signups / pageviews as vanity
Proposes a customer-value North Star tied to the core action
Names input metrics that move the North Star

evals.prompt: We're about to build analytics. Let's just track every click and event so we have all the data later.
evals.expected_output: Instrument only what answers a named question; track-everything is cost and noise. Each event names the question it answers.
expectations: Rejects instrument-everything as cost/noise
Ties each proposed event to a named question it answers
Sizes instrumentation to the stage (less early)

evals.prompt: How are we doing on activation and retention this month?
evals.expected_output: Routes to the user's analytics for the real figures; without the data returns the question to run, not an invented number.
expectations: Does not fabricate activation/retention figures
Routes to the user's own analytics for the numbers
Returns the query/question to run when the data is not in hand

evals.prompt: Our A/B test was planned for 14 days. On day 2 the variant hit p = 0.03 on click-through (a secondary metric); the team wants to stop and ship. What does the reviewer say?
evals.expected_output: Do not ship on that read -- it is peeking. Stopping the moment p < 0.05 during a fixed-horizon test inflates the false-positive rate far above the nominal 5%, so a day-2 hit on a 14-day test is UNVERIFIED, not a win: read a fixed-horizon test once at its pre-committed end (day 14), or switch to a sequential design whose stopping rule matches the looks taken -- an always-valid / anytime-valid bound for continuous monitoring, or a group-sequential / alpha-spending bound for a pre-specified schedule of interim looks. Also, click-through is a SECONDARY metric -- the primary metric and a guardrail must be pre-declared, so a win on a secondary can't be cherry-picked and a regression on the guardrail is caught. If variance is high and a pre-period exists, CUPED-style variance reduction can reach power sooner without abandoning rigor. Ship only on the pre-committed design's read. (growth-analytics/SKILL.md.)
expectations: Identifies stopping on the day-2 p < 0.05 as peeking, which inflates the false-positive rate above the nominal 5% -- the result is UNVERIFIED, not a win

Requires reading a fixed-horizon test once at its pre-committed end, OR a sequential design whose stopping rule matches the looks (always-valid / anytime-valid for continuous monitoring; group-sequential / alpha-spending for a pre-specified interim schedule)
Flags that click-through is a secondary metric; the primary + a guardrail must be pre-declared so a secondary win is not cherry-picked
Does not accept the day-2 result as a ship signal; may note CUPED variance reduction as a rigor-preserving way to reach power sooner

evals.prompt: Signups are up 40% after an ad push, but weekly active users are flat, and the team wants to double the ad budget. What does the analysis recommend?
evals.expected_output: Read the AARRR funnel BOTTOM-UP: retention before acquisition. Flat WAU under rising signups is a retention/activation leak -- pouring more acquisition spend into a leaky bucket is the classic waste. Diagnose in order: is the core action RETAINED? then ACTIVATED? then acquired? Fix why new users do not come back (or do not reach the aha-moment) before scaling acquisition; doubling the ad budget amplifies the leak, it does not fix it. Route the real cohort/retention figures to the user's analytics; do not fabricate a 'good' retention benchmark. (growth-analytics SKILL.md: read AARRR bottom-up, retention first.)
expectations: Reads the funnel bottom-up -- diagnoses retention (and activation) before acquisition
Identifies flat WAU + rising signups as a retention/activation leak; more acquisition into a leaky bucket is waste
Recommends fixing retention before scaling the ad budget (doubling spend amplifies the leak)
Routes real retention/cohort figures to the user's analytics; fabricates no 'good' threshold

evals.prompt: Acme Notes has 40,000 signups and says 8% are active. We want to set next quarter's goal. What should we track?
evals.expected_output: Picks a customer-value North Star, then ends with two or three concrete this-week actions naming the exact events or cohorts to pull and the result that would change the decision; does not end by asking the user to share data; no invented benchmark.
expectations: Rejects raw signups as the goal and names a retained-value metric
Ends with a this-week step naming specific events or cohorts and a decision threshold the team sets
Does not close with 'share your data and I can help'
States no external benchmark as fact

evals.prompt: Acme Notes ran a pricing-page test: 2,000 visitors per arm, control 100 conversions, variant 130, which we call a 50% lift at p<0.01, and a spring email campaign started on day 3. Ship the variant? Give a call.
evals.expected_output: Recomputes the lift from the counts (5.0% to 6.5%, a 30% relative lift, not 50%) and checks the significance claim; names the concurrent campaign as a confounder; gives ONE call (ship, extend to a pre-committed N, or stop); sets a stop tripwire from the stated numbers with a value, a date and an action.
expectations: Leads with the corrected lift figure (about 30% relative) instead of accepting 50%
Names the concurrent email campaign as a confounder
Gives one call, not a menu or a request for more data
Tripwire is derived from the stated rates, with a number, a date and an action, at a level the plan does not already trip
States no external benchmark as fact
